raw_text:
- This research aims to explore why different sites employing the same nominal work procedures experience disparities in completion time. 
- The study will investigate measurable factors that account for these differences and strive to identify observations to differentiate between various explanations.

Assumptions
- It is assumed that measurable factors such as employee characteristics, work environment, and task complexity play a significant role in completion time differences.
- Another assumption is that by employing Bayesian methods, we can update our beliefs about the contributing factors to completion time differences over the course of the study.

Research design
- The study will employ a Bayesian method to update beliefs about the contribution of various factors in completion time differences over time.
- Analysis of site completion times, worker behavior, and task complexities will be conducted to test the hypotheses.

Data or evidence needed
- Data will be collected through surveys and observations of site completion times, worker productivity, and task complexities.
- Evidence will be gathered on the specific factors contributing to the completion time differences for the referred sites.

Measurement
- Completion times will be measured using existing records.
- Worker characteristics and environmental conditions will be measured through surveys.
- Task complexity will be assessed through observations.

Analysis
- A Bayesian statistical model will be applied to test the hypotheses about the contributions of various factors to completion time differences.
- Observations will be used to iteratively update beliefs about the contributing factors.

Decision / stopping rule
- The study will continue until there is a clear consensus among competing factors influencing completion time differences.
- If a particular factor is identified as a consistent contributor to completion time differences, the study will be stopped.

Limitations
- Potential limitations include the possibility of nonresponse bias in survey data and biases caused by observer effect in task complexity measurements.
- Restricted generalizability of the findings to sites not included in the study.
